abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a novel paradigm for processing subgraph isomorphism queries in large-scale graph databases that fundamentally challenges the conventional filter-then-verify architecture. Existing approaches rely on index structures that enumerate candidate subgraphs before performing costly validation, resulting in exponential worst-case complexity. We propose a constraint-propagation framework that integrates pattern matching directly into the filtering phase through a novel algebraic representation we call Graph Constraint Nets (GCN). Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that GCN enables the propagation of structural constraints that eliminate impossible mappings without enumeration, achieving polynomial-time filtering for important classes of graph queries. We formalize the correctness conditions for constraint propagation in this setting and prove that our approach dominates existing techniques in terms of candidate set reduction. Experimental evaluation on real-world graphs containing billions of edges shows that our paradigm reduces candidate enumeration overhead by two to three orders of magnitude while maintaining strong theoretical guarantees. This work opens a new direction for query processing research by demonstrating that fundamentally different algorithmic architectures can provide superior worst-case complexity guarantees for graph database operations.

Approximate query processing (AQP) has emerged as an essential technique for enabling interactive exploration of big data, yet existing probabilistic analysis frameworks provide only loose error bounds that limit practical utility. This paper presents a refined theoretical analysis of variance reduction techniques for online aggregation in data stream environments. We introduce a hierarchical stratified sampling strategy that exploits correlations between query predicates to achieve tighter concentration bounds. Our main theoretical contribution is a novel variance decomposition framework that characterizes the relationship between data distribution skew and estimation accuracy for aggregation queries with arbitrary filter conditions. We prove that our approach achieves error bounds that are asymptotically tighter than state-of-the-art techniques by a factor of O(sqrt(n)) for skewed distributions. Furthermore, we derive optimal sample allocation strategies under memory constraints using this framework. Extensive analysis on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrates that our theoretical improvements translate into practical performance gains, reducing query execution time by 40-60% while maintaining statistical guarantees.

This paper introduces Helios, a distributed main-memory database system designed for cloud-native deployment that reimagines transaction processing through a novel separation of concerns architecture. Conventional distributed databases interleave concurrency control with data placement decisions, leading to performance bottlenecks when scaling across geo-distributed cloud regions. Helios decouples these concerns by introducing a两层 architecture consisting of logically centralized transaction coordination supported by physically distributed data storage. The transaction coordinator implements a re-designed optimistic concurrency control protocol that exploits commutative operation semantics to maximize parallelism while guaranteeing serializability. We present the complete system architecture including novel techniques for dynamic workload-aware data migration, adaptive thread management for heterogeneous cloud infrastructure, and crash recovery protocols that maintain sub-second failover times. Our implementation handles petabyte-scale datasets across 500+ nodes with linear scalability. Comprehensive evaluation using the TPC-C benchmark and real-world OLTP workloads demonstrates that Helios achieves 3.5x throughput improvement over existing systems while reducing cross-region latency by 60%.

We present AdaptiveCache, an improved storage engine architecture for large-scale data warehousing that significantly advances the state of the art in columnar data management. While existing columnar databases achieve excellent compression through dictionary encoding, they suffer from inefficient point update handling that requires expensive decompression and recompression cycles. AdaptiveCache introduces a novel dual-format storage model that maintains both columnar and row-group representations with automatic format conversion based on access patterns. The system incorporates a learned cost model that predicts optimal storage format configurations by analyzing query workloads in real-time. Key technical contributions include a lightweight metadata tracking mechanism for format conversion, a work-stealing scheduler for background reorganization tasks, and an intelligent prefetching strategy for mixed workloads. We detail the complete implementation including integration with Apache Parquet and integration points for query optimizers. Performance evaluation on TPC-DS benchmarks with 100TB data scale demonstrates 2-4x improvement in mixed analytical and transactional workloads while maintaining compression ratios comparable to state-of-the-art columnar systems.
